article.title: Chuck Schumer’s Former Aides Now Lobby for Corporate America
article.author: Branko Marcetic
article.content: One of the quirks of Sen. Chuck Schumer’s (D-NY) bid to lead the incoming Democratic Senate majority is that delivering the change voters demanded in November would mean facing off against a small army of his own former staff. Over his many years in Congress, Schumer has seen countless staffers cycle into his office and out into lobbying work for a broad swath of corporate interests: banks, credit card companies, health insurers, drugmakers, cryptocurrency firms, and the AI industry. His former top health advisor lobbies for the American Medical Association, a longtime opponent of single-payer health care. His ex-chief counsel now leads a top lobbying firm’s AI practice as lawmakers weigh how to regulate the industry. Two former financial advisors now lobby for a crypto industry eager to win government-backed legitimacy while keeping the government off its back. Two former legislative directors have lobbied for the private equity industry on housing legislation. A search of federal lobbying disclosures filed since the start of 2025 turns up upwards of a thousand reports naming former Schumer staffers. For his rival for the leadership spot , Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) — like Schumer, a decades-long creature of the DC establishment — the equivalent number is only a fraction of this. The disclosures show a different mix of clients: an airline, a major university, several local airport-related organizations, and a company that develops drones for delivering food and medicine, to name a few. It’s all part of a Washington practice Schumer has excelled at: building a vast network of former staff whose careers he takes an interest in long after they’ve left his office. “People come into Washington in their twenties and thirties, go to the private sector, but stay tethered to their former boss. And the rising tide lifts all boats,” says Jeff Hauser, executive director of the Revolving Door Project. Schumer’s current staff “get extra mentorship from the alumni who are strewn across DC lobbying for various industries,” Hauser says, sometimes simply about benign matters like how to handle their boss. But the resulting close network of loyal former staffers can also be a rich resource in a town that runs on who you know. “These people are super valuable if you’re a corporate interest and looking for who to hire,” he says. This is the fundamental conundrum of Schumer’s potential leadership: if elected majority leader again, the longtime New York senator will have to make good on a historic mandate for change by challenging the very industries that have hired some of his own former senior staff to represent them. Medicare for Few Take, for instance, Matt Fuentes, a partner at the Democratic lobbying firm Avenue Solutions, whose former role as Schumer’s senior health policy adviser for eight years is prominently advertised on the firm’s website. Since 2025, Fuentes has been a lobbyist for the American Medical Association (AMA), a longtime opponent of single-payer health care that has fought national health insurance proposals for more than a century . The AMA has softened its stance in recent years, but its policymaking body voted in 2023 to retain its opposition to single payer . Fuentes doesn’t just lobby for the AMA. His clients include a broad swath of the for-profit health care industry, including some of the large drugmakers Merck, Moderna, Takeda, and Amgen, as well as pharmacy services company HouseRx. His client list also features insurers Blue Cross Blue Shield and UnitedHealth Group (UHG). For the latter, he has lobbied on “prior authorization” — the widely disliked insurer practice of requiring advance approval for care, which can delay treatment and sometimes have deadly consequences. Records show that, for both insurers, Fuentes lobbied on AI and its “correlation to prior authorization and utilization management policies.” UHG and other insurers have long come under fire for the controversial practice of using AI to deny care to and overcharge people, with UHG specifically the subject of a lawsuit alleging it used an algorithm to deny care to older patients. That is one kind of AI use the incoming Congress might seek to regulate. Then there’s Reggie Babin, whose former role in Schumer’s office is prominently displayed on his page on Akin Gump’s website. Babin is co-lead of the firm’s federal AI policy practice. In practice, that means Babin — who worked for five years under Schumer, two of them as his chief counsel from 2020 to 2022 — has lobbied Congress on data centers and AI regulation for several companies, including Microsoft , Adobe , Dropbox , and data center operator STACK Infrastructure . His clients also include OpenAI , the maker of ChatGPT, and the Data Center Coalition, a trade group for data center operators whose board of directors includes executives from across the industry. A 2025 filing lists Babin as lobbying on the coalition’s behalf on “issues related to Section 232 investigations and investment,” a reference to the Trump administration’s trade investigations under Section 232. Tariffs threatened to raise the cost of the AI data center buildout. The concerns about staffers-turned-lobbyists like Fuentes and Babin aren’t theoretical. As the American Prospect reported at the time, a package of antitrust bills aimed at tech giants had broad bipartisan and public support during Joe Biden’s presidency. Schumer, then Senate majority leader, never brought the bills to the floor. “How did the enormous momentum against Big Tech that was developed at the end of the 2010s and built in the early days of the Biden administration fail to lead to significant legislative changes?” says Hauser. “Schumer’s daughters and many former staffers working in Big Tech is a popular explanation.” The New York Post reported at the time that not only were Schumer’s two daughters an Amazon lobbyist and a Facebook product marketing manager, but eighty of his former staffers had gone on to take jobs at those and numerous other tech companies, including Google and Apple. That included Babin, who moved on after the 117th Congress to Akin Gump, which raked in millions of dollars in lobbying fees from tech firms. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who was championing the legislation, blamed unnamed members of Congress for “giving in to the dominant social media platforms,” while a former Senate staffer told HuffPost that “if Schumer wanted this to happen it would have already happened.” The Prospect reported that Schumer said the votes weren’t there, though he hadn’t conducted a private whip count. Super Intelligence Babin is just one of Schumer’s former senior staff who today lobbies for the AI industry. Another is Lucia Panza, Schumer’s former leadership counsel. She took a position lobbying for Amazon after leaving the Senate and now represents companies before Congress and other federal bodies at Crossroads Strategies. When Panza joined the firm, its CEO noted that “her time advising some of the most influential lawmakers and voices in Washington, D.C.” would be helpful to their clients. During Trump’s second term, her clients have included AI companies and other businesses and trade groups that lobby on AI, such as Motorola and the Advanced Medical Technology Association. One of the AI firms Panza has represented is CoreWeave, a cloud computing firm whose bonds have come under pressure amid concerns about the AI data center buildout on which its business depends. Like Babin, Panza also counts the Data Center Coalition as a client. Records show that Panza began lobbying on the Ratepayer Protection Act for both the coalition and CoreWeave in the third quarter of 2026. The bill would require state regulators and certain utilities to consider standards for recovering grid upgrade costs from large data centers. It passed the House 417–3 in September and met opposition in the Senate . A separate bill addressing data center costs passed the Senate in November , leaving the question of who pays for grid upgrades on the congressional agenda. This is on top of several other Schumer connections knee-deep in the industry. Grace Magaletta, his legislative correspondent from 2019 to 2023, lobbied for Samsung on “artificial intelligence policy issues” as recently as 2025. Josh Vlasto, who worked for Schumer from 2004 to 2010, this election cycle co-headed an AI industry group funding Democratic and Republican super PACs to help elect candidates friendly to the industry. Throughout Trump’s second term, Schumer’s former communications director, Israel “Izzy” Klein — whose firm trumpets his “deep ties to congressional leadership” and who was appointed in October to the Congressional Award’s board of directors by Schumer — has lobbied for Cisco and Larry Ellison’s Oracle. Resolution Public Affairs, whose principals included former Schumer legislative directors Heather McHugh and Meghan Taira, also employed a third former Schumer staffer. The three lobbied for chipmaker TSMC Arizona, a key part of the AI supply chain, and on AI issues for Oracle and the Murdoch family’s News Corp. Maxwell Young, who served several stints in Schumer’s office over the past two decades, including most recently as his senior communications adviser in 2020, has since November 2025 been the head of policy communications for AI giant Anthropic. In September, OpenAI hired Schumer’s daughter away from Amazon to head its lobbying efforts at the state and local levels in the Northeast. Not all of Schumer’s ex-staffers are simply doing the industry’s bidding. Carrie Adams, Schumer’s deputy digital director from January 2017 to June 2018, now lobbies for the AI Policy Network (AIPN). She lobbies Congress and, as of the third quarter of 2026, federal agencies including the State, Treasury, and Commerce Departments on a range of AI issues. AIPN, which has gotten funding from ultrarich AI safety advocates and describes itself as independent, backs more regulation as well as export controls aimed at keeping the United States ahead of China in the AI “race.” Political Currency Former Schumer staffers also work for the cryptocurrency industry as it seeks mainstream legitimacy. One example is Jennifer Brown, a former financial policy adviser to Schumer. After Brown left Schumer’s office in 2025, crypto investment firm Paradigm added her to its Policy Council . In announcing the new members, Paradigm said it wanted to “put the misguided era of anti-crypto policy firmly in the rearview mirror,” just months after the Senate leader — while being advised by her — had failed to extend the tenure of a crypto-skeptical SEC commissioner before Trump was sworn in. Brown joined BGR Group as a lobbyist in January 2025, focusing on financial regulation and tax policy. The firm highlighted her experience under Schumer when it announced her hiring. Many of those issues involve cryptocurrency. Filings list Brown as lobbying for crypto clients including stablecoin issuer Circle, wallet provider Phantom, and crypto-focused investors Dragonfly and Digital Currency Group. Brown also lobbied on crypto regulation in 2025 and 2026 for the Decentralization Research Center, which advocates for keeping cryptocurrency “decentralized” — in other words, free from the control of a single authority, including governments and banks. A Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) memo from September 2025 detailed how members of both the center and BGR (Brown wasn’t listed as an attendee) met with the SEC’s Crypto Task Force to discuss regulation of the crypto industry, and handed them reading materials about decentralization. Brown also lobbied for venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, headed by billionaire Marc Andreessen, maybe best known as one of the first and most high-profile Silicon Valley oligarchs to shift his allegiance from Democrats to MAGA. Andreessen Horowitz employed Brown to lobby on AI and digital assets. It was one of several of Brown’s clients, like data center operator Galaxy Digital Holdings, that sit at the intersection of crypto and AI. Brown is one of several former senior Schumer staffers who have lobbied for crypto-related clients. That the crypto world will have the possible next Senate majority leader’s allies as its advocates in Congress comes at a pivotal time for the industry, which has sought to shed its reputation for facilitating scams and become a mainstream investment option while remaining as free from government oversight as possible. To get there, the industry has pushed for a Goldilocks-style regulatory regime: just enough to grant it legitimacy and reassure skeptical Americans that buying digital assets is safe, but not enough to seriously step on its toes. But that effort has also aroused concern from experts, who fear the destabilizing effects of having digital assets under a light regulatory touch reshaping the balance sheets of banks and other financial institutions. The collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s FTX in 2022 seemed to be a cautionary tale, an episode whose fallout was largely contained within the crypto sector. Under Trump, the industry has moved aggressively to deepen its links to the broader financial system. One former Schumer staffer’s lobbying record illustrates the crypto industry’s push for legitimacy through regulation: Ryan Eagan, the Crypto Council for Innovation’s (CCI) director of US federal affairs, whose nearly decade-long stint advising Schumer on banking policy is the first thing mentioned in his official bio, along with his work with other members of Congress to “advance legislative priorities” like “cryptocurrency policies.” In 2026, Eagan lobbied on a spate of bills for the CCI that illustrate the industry’s “just right” regulatory framework: bills extending established securities and commodities tax rules to digital assets or cracking down on fraud and terrorist financing in the industry, as well as a bill barring the Federal Reserve from issuing a central bank digital currency, a measure criticized for potentially putting a straitjacket on monetary policy in a future economic crisis. One bill, the GENIUS Act, which Trump signed into law in July 2025, requires payment stablecoins to be backed by liquid assets such as dollars or short-term US Treasuries. A 2026 working paper argues that a growing stablecoin market could add to systemic risk by tying stablecoin redemptions to the functioning of the Treasury market. A number of other bills Eagan lobbied on were similarly controversial. The CLARITY Act, along with several other pieces of legislation listed in the lobbying filings involving Eagan, would give the smaller Commodity Futures Trading Commission authority over trading in digital commodities and retain a role for the SEC in regulating securities. The CLARITY Act passed the House in July 2025 with a large bipartisan majority. In September 2026, a Senate vote to advance it failed , 49–50 — but the industry is already planning to run it back in the new, Democratic-led Congress next year, with one expert observing that the midterm result doesn’t mean the bill is dead, but that it simply “changes the authors of the next draft.” Schumer’s fellow New York senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a prominent backer of crypto legislation, has drawn scrutiny for her ties to the industry. The crypto connections do not end there. Filings show that Panza, Schumer’s former leadership counsel, has lobbied on the GENIUS and CLARITY Acts for fintech company Block Inc., credit card trade group Electronic Payments Coalition, and the Financial Services Forum, an industry group representing eight of the largest US financial institutions. (She also lobbied on general crypto issues for Visa and the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association.) The trio of former Schumer staffers at Resolution Public Affairs likewise lobbied for these two bills for asset manager BlackRock and JPMorgan Chase. Return of Wall Street Meanwhile, several of these same former staffers now also lobby for a financial sector that has long stood in the way of reform in Congress and that many Americans associate with corruption in Washington. The Resolution Public Affairs trio, for instance, lobbied throughout this year for the American Investment Council (AIC), a private equity trade group that fought Joe Biden’s proposed tax hikes in 2021. Among other things, they lobbied on the AIC’s behalf on housing legislation that included limits on purchases of single-family homes by large institutional investors. The federal government enacted those limits in July 2026. The Private Equity Stakeholder Project separately estimates that private equity firms own at least a tenth of US apartments. Besides lobbying for both JPMorgan Chase and Mastercard on the matter of capping credit card rates, they also counted as a client the Investment Company Institute (ICI). They lobbied on a bill the ICI supported that aimed to make it harder to treat nonbank institutions as systemic risks to the economy that need extra regulatory scrutiny. Likewise, Panza has spent Trump’s second term lobbying for a number of finance clients on regulatory issues, including work for Morgan Stanley on the implementation of the Obama-era Dodd-Frank Act. Some also represent the growing gambling industry, which has poured money into politics and lobbying . Jennifer Brown, Schumer’s former banking counsel, has lobbied over the past two years for FanDuel on “federal gaming policy,” while Schumer’s two former legislative directors, Heather McHugh and Meghan Taira, lobbied in 2026 through Resolution Public Affairs for the prediction market platform Kalshi. The reason Taira, who spent a total of eighteen years in Schumer’s office, is no longer at the firm is because in October she cut out the middleman and went to work for Kalshi directly, heading its federal lobbying efforts. It was part of a hiring spree of former Democratic staffers that the company undertook in the lead-up to the GOP’s bloodbath this November. Schumer vs. His Own Staffers It would be easy to say this is simply what happens when you’ve been in Washington for a long time. Schumer’s rival, Van Hollen, has represented Maryland in Congress since 2003, and his former staffers’ lobbying work tells a different story. Some former Van Hollen staffers do represent companies with a stake in the incoming Congress’s agenda. Cassandra Brzezinski, a Van Hollen policy adviser until January 2026, now lobbies for Allstate Insurance, the Financial Technology Association, and the London Stock Exchange Group, the latter on digital assets and AI. John Mitchell, his former legislative aide, lobbied in 2025 for Workday, which sells human resources software that uses AI. Alexander Simpson, a legislative correspondent for Van Hollen when he served in the House, now lobbies for American Airlines. The Van Hollen alumni in the filings generally held less senior positions and represented a different mix of clients. Schumer’s alumni include a former chief counsel and multiple former legislative directors working for some of the biggest companies in health care, finance, and technology. The next Democratic Senate majority leader will have a long to-do list, from expanding Medicare and regulating AI and crypto to lowering housing costs as large financial firms buy up more of the nation’s homes. If Schumer wins back the majority leadership, it may prove the most compelling test yet of just how much influence the Washington revolving door commands. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
